mcqs.question: make_adder(5) returns a closure over n. If it were possible to later reassign n inside make_adder's scope after the closure was created, what would the closure see on its next call?
options: A TypeError, since closures cannot reference reassignable variables
The updated value, because the closure holds a live reference to the variable, not a snapshot taken at creation time
The value from the very first call only, cached forever after that
The original value 5, because closures capture a snapshot at creation time
mcqs.explanation: A closure captures a reference to the variable itself, not a copy of its value at closure-creation time — so any later reassignment of that variable is visible on the closure's next read. There's no snapshotting and no exception involved.

mcqs.question: makeCounter() is called twice, producing counter and counter2. Why does calling counter() several times not affect what counter2() returns?
options: Because count is declared with a special private keyword
It's a coincidence of this specific example; in general two closures from the same factory do share state
Because each call to makeCounter() creates a fresh count variable and a fresh closure over it, so the two closures are entirely independent
Because JavaScript automatically resets closures between function calls
mcqs.explanation: Every invocation of the outer factory function creates a brand-new local variable and a brand-new closure capturing it — there's no keyword involved and no sharing between separate invocations. This independence is the whole mechanism, not a special case.

mcqs.question: Under lexical scoping, how does a variable reference inside a function get resolved?
options: Based on where the function is written in the source, regardless of where or how it's later called
Based on the local variables of whichever function calls it at runtime
Based on whichever variable of that name was most recently assigned anywhere in the program
Based on the type of the variable, resolved at compile time only
mcqs.explanation: Lexical scoping resolves references according to the function's position in the source text at definition time — that's what makes closures predictable just by reading the code. Resolving against the caller's locals is dynamic scoping, a different and much rarer model.

mcqs.question: Why does replacing var with let in the classic for-loop-plus-setTimeout example fix the bug?
options: let disables closures entirely inside loops
let is function-scoped, so it avoids creating any closures
let makes setTimeout run synchronously instead of asynchronously
let is block-scoped, so the loop creates a distinct binding of the variable on every iteration for each closure to capture
mcqs.explanation: let's block scoping means each loop iteration gets its own separate binding, so each callback's closure captures a different variable holding a different value. It doesn't disable closures, doesn't change scoping to function-level, and has no effect on setTimeout's async behavior.

mcqs.question: A long-lived event listener's closure captures an entire large API response object just to read one field from it. What's the memory consequence?
options: None — garbage collectors always free unused fields even if the closure still references the parent object
The whole object is kept alive for as long as the listener is registered, not just the field that's actually used
Only the specific field is kept alive; the rest of the object is freed automatically
The object is copied into a smaller structure containing only the used field
mcqs.explanation: A closure keeps alive whatever variable it references, not a minimal slice of it — so capturing the whole object keeps the whole object reachable and un-collectible for as long as the closure exists. Garbage collectors free unreachable memory, and this object is still reachable through the closure.

mcqs.question: An interviewer asks you to fix three callbacks in a loop that all print the same final value, but the language has no block-scoped binding available. Which fix still works?
options: Wrap the loop body in a function that takes the loop variable as a parameter, so each call gets its own fresh copy to close over
Add a global counter that each callback reads at call time instead of the loop variable
Move all the callbacks outside the loop and call them manually afterward
Nothing can fix it without block scoping — the bug is unavoidable in such a language
mcqs.explanation: Passing the loop variable as a parameter to an immediately-invoked wrapper function manufactures a fresh binding per iteration by hand — exactly what block-scoped let does automatically. A global counter reproduces the same shared-state bug, moving the callbacks doesn't address the shared-variable capture, and the bug is fixable without block scoping.
